To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

JND for natural frequency of a virtual second order dynamic system can be as low as 3.99 %, that JND is lower when participants actively excite the virtual system, and that JND is not significantly different between active and passive perception.

1) the JND for natural frequency is 3.99% to 6.99% of the reference frequency, 2) visual feedback improves the discrimination performance in passive perception, 3) active perception does not improve the JND compared to passive perception, and 4) the stiffness of the virtual spring does not affect the discrimination performance.
the JND for natural frequency of second order dynamic systems is 6.96 %, 6.02 %, and 3.99 %, respectively, for reference frequencies of two, two and a half, and three hertz, respectively.

the JND of natural frequency for second order dynamic systems and how the JND is affected by sensory feedback and active perception.
the JND for natural frequency of dynamic systems.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the JND for natural frequency of a second-order system is 3.99% - 6.96% and is independent of the stiffness of the system.
the human JND for natural frequency of a dynamic system is not influenced by the maximum force experienced during interaction with that system.

the JND for natural frequency is significantly affected by sensory feedback, with the combination of visual and haptic sensory feedback resulting in the best discrimination performance in passive perception.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
JND is smaller when the participant actively perceives the natural frequency, and that the JND is smaller with haptic feedback.
the JND for natural frequency of a virtual dynamic system is in the range of 4 % to 7 %, and the JND is affected significantly by the sensory feedback provided during perception.
human participants are able to perceive natural frequencies of virtual second order systems with JND of 6.96 %.
The main takeaway from our work is that
natural frequency can be discriminated with a small JND, which is comparable to the JND for natural frequency in physical systems.
JND for virtual resonance tasks can be estimated with haptic devices.
the JND for natural frequency of a virtual dynamic system is similar to that of a physical system, and that sensory feedback and active perception can improve JND performance.
